item.title: Flock’s CEO admits to an abuse problem
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: Flock reportedly has an abuse problem. Its CEO admitted to it, but his response may leave you unsatisfied.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Police officers across the US are being accused of using Flock’s license plate cameras to stalk people, per a Washington Post report yesterday. Last week, Flock CEO Garrett Langley conceded to The Drive that “the abuse is a problem”—but his explanation of what the company is doing about it may leave people unsatisfied.

What happened: At least 50 police officers have been charged with—or accused of—using license plate readers for unauthorized purposes like stalking people (46 of whom used Flock’s system), per the Post.

Here are just some of the company’s recent controversies, many of which came to light in the past month:

  • Last May, police in Texas used Flock to look for a woman suspected of self-managing an abortion. The search included 83,000 cameras, some in states where abortion is legal. The sheriff defended it as a welfare check.
  • The Drive reporter who later interviewed Langley was a victim himself: He was boxed in by police cars outside a Kohl’s after a data entry error flagged the car he was driving as stolen. (Separately, an analysis of 2023 and 2024 data found that Flock misread license plates in 71% of the alerts it sent to police in Roseville, CA.)
  • In Milwaukee, an officer illegally ran a partner’s plate 124 times; the detective assigned to investigate that officer was himself charged with Flock misuse.
  • A 404 Media review found that police departments across the US have used Flock cameras hundreds of times to search for specific people instead of cars, sometimes referencing a person’s race or political affiliation.

Let’s get physical: Backlash against Flock has been increasing, and it’s even taken to the streets—protesters have thrown paint on cameras, snipped their wires, printed 3D objects to obstruct their view, and put trash bags over them. In one non-destructive protest, a 77-year-old in St. Petersburg, FL, blocked a camera with a sign taped to a pool skimmer reading “Down with Flock cameras” (in all caps). At least six cities have deactivated the cameras or canceled their contracts with Flock.

Langley acknowledged the problem in the interview with The Drive and pointed to the company’s existing guardrails, but stopped short of specifics when asked about future ones. The company told the Post it “will soon be announcing better filters and tools to stop abuse before it happens.”

Bottom line: “Over a million cases were solved last year with this technology, and the level of abuse is incredibly low relative to that,” Langley said. Which is a fair point, until you run the math—at roughly 20 billion plate scans a month, “incredibly low” still affects a lot of people. —LC

item.title: Google Earth, now with a side of potentially harmful fantasy
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Google Earth’s new AI image generation feature can turn a text prompt into photorealistic satellite imagery. People are concerned.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: A new AI image generation feature now lives inside Google Earth. An independent researcher found that it’s trivially easy to abuse, letting you create realistic satellite images of violent or politically inflammatory scenes, despite the company saying it has guardrails.

What happened: With a simple prompt, you can now generate AI images that drop fake structures, people, or events over Google’s satellite imagery. The new feature went live yesterday in Google Earth using Nano Banana 2—and it’s a puzzling add-on to a go-to tool often used in education and by open-source intelligence analysts and journalists.

While making realistic-looking deepfakes of satellite images was possible before, this AI feature does it in one step (often in just a minute)—and results can be refined to look more convincing. You can probably see the potential danger from space, and journalists and researchers are already voicing their concerns.

What could go wrong?: Google’s own pitch for the tool is benign—recreating historical places or visualizing a real estate project using the actual topography before you break ground. Its blog post encourages you to “let your imagination run wild,” but that’s exactly the worry.

Researcher Henk van Ess found that a single sentence was enough to place a nuclear power plant in Iran, drop a crowd of refugees near the US-Mexico border, or even depict a fatal crash on an Amsterdam street. 404 Media reported it was able to add both a homeless encampment and a bomb blast crater in Los Angeles.

Google’s response: In a statement to van Ess, Google said it takes misinformation seriously and that “every image created with Nano Banana in Google Earth includes the SynthID digital watermark.” But detecting that watermark, which is invisible to the human eye, takes an extra step—either asking Gemini or using Google Lens to see if the image is fake. (There’s also a Gemini watermark on every image, but it’s easy to crop out.) And when van Ess posted a screen recording of his fake imagery on X, a popular third-party AI detector gave it just a 0.8% likelihood of being AI.

Google also said it prevents “image creation on harmful topics,” but van Ess reports that none of the prompts he tried were refused. As of publication time, Tech Brew could still prompt the tool to place a nuclear plant in Iran without any objection.

Bottom line: Google says there are guardrails in place. But given everything, it’s unclear what it counts as a harmful topic. In an age of so much disinformation, having an AI image generator inside this reputable digital atlas sounds like a recipe for disaster. —WK

Also at Google…

  • Finally! One of Chrome’s most annoying update features could be gone soon.

item.title: Avoiding the AI traffic jam
item.dc:creator: Morning Brew Creative Studio
item.description: Managers shouldn’t feel like they’re stuck in a busy intersection directing projects. See how Smartsheet helps break up AI silos and sends you cruising down easy street.
item.content:encoded:
TOGETHER WITH

AI at the crossroads: Managers are stuck cleaning up traffic jams caused by disconnected AI tools. Smartsheet helps you get the wheels moving again

AI was supposed to handle managers’ busywork. So why does the day-to-day still feel like gridlock?

Managing siloed AI tools gets exhausting when it adds countless decisions to your day-to-day. It can feel like directing traffic when you should be looking at the bigger picture.

No one at the office wants to feel like a traffic cop dealing with a busy intersection. That’s where Smartsheet can help. Their MCP integration is designed to let AI talk and act directly with your work tools. That way, a prompt for a project becomes workflows, timelines, and status updates that build themselves. Before we get too deeply into how they do it, let’s talk a little bit about why they do.

The intersection of frustration and repetition

A day in the life of a manager with disjointed AI tools isn’t dissimilar to that of a traffic cop. It requires constant vigilance, responding to dozens of simultaneously changing signals, and communicating with all the drivers. Every draft from Claude or report from ChatGPT requires a human to manually translate and route it between systems, which just adds administrative overhead.

Every time a car (work you want AI to help with) pulls up, the manager needs to stop that car (review and assess) and help it get to where it needs to go (send it to the next system). That’s fine when you have to do it once a day. The car goes by, you help it along, and you get back to your other duties.

The danger is when you scale up, and multiple projects zip around at once. For the traffic cop manager, that means dozens of cars every day, all with their own drivers going different speeds. On top of that, there are pedestrians crossing (collaborating with an outside team) and drivers forgoing turn signals (deliverables sitting in the wrong place). Or the truly unexpected strikes, like a horse walking into the middle of the road (sudden strategy changes).

All the elements of a stressful day come together, creating a big mess—and everyone else slows down to look at the big mess on the road, creating more traffic. Then there’s another manager doing the same thing with their intersection, and the problem compounds. It’s not what anyone signed up for, and there has to be a better way than directly handling every little thing.

Intelligence as an accelerator

So, enough catastrophizing. Much like the technological innovation that is the mighty stoplight, Smartsheet provides intelligent coordination.

Take the manager acting as a traffic cop out of the equation, and sub in the Smartsheet stoplight. Now there are ways to connect the systems and provide context. For a stoplight, sensors under the ground, cameras, and even the pedestrian walk button all provide key information to keep everyone moving. Smartsheet operates on the same principle.

Instead of routing instead of translating context between your systems and your AI tools yourself, Smartsheet’s AI assistant can understand live project data and take action through conversation. It can ask about risks, update statuses, and generate reports. That gives projects the green light to get where they need to be. Because the AI assistant works directly with the operational system, there’s no translation step—just connected systems communicating with each other and improving upon themselves.

So let’s reframe this in an office setting. You ask Claude to draft a kickoff plan. Then it appears in your tracker, ready to go. As the project runs, Claude can evaluate enterprise data and surface risks instantly. After that, it can pull a portfolio summary in seconds, with real-time insights across your business.

What about that horse?

Surely, AI can’t account for a horse in the road, a sudden strategy pivot, or any other kind of curveball. That’s what managers are for.

By eliminating the manual context-shuffling, you shift from managing AI outputs to managing work, stepping in to handle the horse so everything else doesn’t grind to a halt. That’s hard to do when you’re bogged down in every step-by-step operation instead of coming up for air to address the bigger issues.

Traffic cop life isn’t the only option. For those who prefer a smarter way of working, one that even allows for a coffee and donut break every now and then, look no further than Smartsheet.

item.title: Meta's big AI win isn't its models or chatbots
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Meta’s most recent earnings report didn’t show much of a payoff on its giant AI spending. Its biggest win: increasing time spent on Instagram and selling more ads.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Meta’s latest earnings show that, for all its sprawling AI ambitions, its core business really is still about selling our attention. One of its clearest wins last quarter was that people couldn’t put Instagram down, boosting ad revenue—which isn’t much to show for a year of record AI spending.

What happened: You’re not alone if your Reels habit recently hit cry-for-help levels. This past quarter, the amount of time people spent on Instagram jumped by double digits year over year, Meta says.

Mark Zuckerberg credited our collectively worsening scrolling habit to an improved AI-powered algorithm. Every public Reel and feed post on Instagram is now being analyzed by LLMs to recommend content better, according to the company—with AI also enabling better targeted ads. (Though all this probably doesn’t help the “Instagram is addictive by design” accusations.)

In other words, the clearest way that AI is making money for Meta is keeping eyeballs on feeds longer, which in turn sells more ads—though the firm’s overall profits still fell about 14% compared to this time last year.

All in on ads: Advertising made up a whopping $59.4 billion of Meta’s $60.8 billion total revenue last quarter. And it’s clearly trying to lean into its biggest moneymaker: The company’s building out an AI-powered, automated one-stop shop for brands to create and serve ads (though the rollout’s been mixed). Meanwhile, its Reality Labs division—where its popular smart glasses and not-so-popular VR headsets are developed—continued to hemorrhage money despite growing revenue, losing $4.6 billion last quarter.

Meta’s AI media blitz: The lack of a bigger AI payoff also helps explain Zuck’s recent “AI optimist” press tour—which included an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal basically subtweeting OpenAI and Anthropic. And while others in the AI industry, including those at major labs, want to “deliberately pace” frontier AI development, Meta’s CEO evidently isn’t a fan of slowing down (perhaps because it could make it harder for Meta to catch up).

Bottom line: Meta positions itself as an AI company building “superintelligence.” But its recent financial results show that the smartest thing its AI currently does might be picking your next Reel. —WK

Also at Meta…

  • Zuck makes a bold prediction about AI agents—and he’s betting the company’s future on it.

item.title: Lease is more
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Apple’s new hardware leasing program offers 12- to 36-month leases on iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple Watches—costing customers less than their retail prices.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: You can now rent a new iPhone for less than what an ad-free Netflix subscription costs per month. Apple’s leasing program lands just as memory-related price hikes ripple across tech, including Apple’s own already-pricey lineup—but it’s still a lot of money for hardware you might not ever own.

What to know: Apple Upgrade is the company’s first consumer hardware leasing program—not a financing option, like the old iPhone Upgrade was. The big benefit: Leasing costs less than buying outright. A base model iPhone 17e, for example, might set you back $17.99 a month on a 24-month lease. That adds up to $431.76 over two years, while the phone’s current retail price is $599. When your lease ends, you can buy the phone by paying off its remaining cost, upgrade, roll onto a month‑to‑month lease for up to six months, or just return it and bid it adieu.

Buy now, pay later platform Klarna provides the lease itself, which won’t do a hard pull on your credit report. Payments are interest free, with no late fees. As for that mysterious iOS code spotted last week, which seemed to allude to leased iPhones with missed payments getting remotely restricted—Apple says that won’t be the case.

Here’s the nitty-gritty:

  • You can lease iPhones and Apple Watches for 12 or 24 months; Macs and iPads for 24 or 36.
  • Apple Upgrade is US-only for now.
  • You have to return the device in “good working condition” or eat a damage fee. (AppleCare+ is available as an add-on, though.)
  • You can bail early, but you’ll pay a termination fee (as in, the total of your remaining lease payments). You’ll also have to return the device within 14 days.
  • Miss three payments in a row, and the lease will terminate, with the full outstanding balance coming due.

The mutual upside: For Apple, leasing keeps new hardware moving despite price hikes that might otherwise have dented sales—and builds a pipeline of returned units it can refurbish and resell for a profit (one that might outweigh what it loses on leases). For consumers, renting can beat buying an Apple product outright, as it’s cheaper and you can then upgrade once the lease ends. Though you’re spending hundreds on hardware you may never own and forfeit the resale value Apple gear is famous for.

Bottom line: Apple Upgrade makes the company’s products more affordable—at the cost of real ownership. But given that everything else is already a monthly subscription, it might be a bargain many eagerly grab. —WK

item.title: Google exec says link lists aren’t going away as search transforms
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: Google VP of Search Liz Reid discussed how the search experience is changing in the AI era and what it means for the internet as a whole.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, AI has fundamentally changed what it means to google something—and the transformation isn’t done.

The search engine made a slew of announcements at its developer conference earlier this year that included the first change to the search box in a quarter century. The upshot is a more AI-centric experience with options for news alert-style information agents that automatically scour the web for you.

Though Google has clarified that the familiar list of links isn’t going away, multiple headlines have called it the end of search as we know it. But Reid insisted that Google still cares about the health of the internet as a whole.

“Search is not a useful product if the web is not a thriving product, and so I think we probably care about that more than any other company in the world,” Google VP of Search Liz Reid told us.

We spoke with Reid about what this means for how you browse the web, what it means for websites that depend on Google for survival, and how it will change the ads you see.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Do you think that there’s a time in the future, amid all this AI change, that the familiar list of links could go away entirely? Or that there could be a different format for funneling users to the web?

I don’t see any time in which the links go away. I think what we actually see is that people don’t want AI or the web; they want both. There’s a lot of topics where AI really gets you started, and then people want to engage more. They value the expertise, the opinions, the taste of how to think about a particular topic. This is a time in which AI is growing, and it’s a time in which newsletters and podcasts and videos and all these new formats seem to also be blossoming because people really want to hear that expertise. So we want to continue to make that thrive.

We have for a long time continued to innovate on how you can surface links on the web. So we have the blue links, but we have, at times, we have the top stories part. We have what people are saying in AI Mode and in AI Overviews.

If we know users want to connect to that information, how do we make it as easy as possible? How do we make it as seamless as possible? And we’ll continue to innovate and we announced some updates pretty recently on how we’re showcasing links in additional ways. But I think that is kind of what makes search at its heart—not just knowing the information about the web, but connecting people to content on the web. And I don’t see that going away.

Obviously, online publishers are seeing click-through rates decline with these changes, and some publishers are even considering blocking all Google crawlers. In terms of making sure that the open web is still a healthy place to supply these AI tools and search, how do you think about that in the long term?

We do spend a lot of time thinking about this. We try to really design our AI experiences in sort of a web-forward way. We have teams whose job is to think about: What are great links to surface more effectively? How do you show them in a way that’s great for folks? We’ve innovated; one example is in AI Overviews, we’ll now often show on some timely stories, a big carousel of publishers that we didn’t have three months ago. So we’re constantly trying to figure out how we innovate on that.

The good news is that people still want to connect with other people’s content, and so we can facilitate that. And as long as people make great content that other people want to read, then we believe we can continue to foster that.

Companies like Microsoft are experimenting with publisher marketplaces or other compensation schemes. Is that something you’re considering?

We have a blog post in which we’ve talked about some of the various news deals and other things we have.

We have a variety of different ways—we have a long history of deals with news and others for great content. In general, we’re all still—I mean, at times it can feel like a long time—but we’re still pretty early in the space, and so continue to innovate.

In terms of the revenue side, how has this changed Google’s ad model? Do you feel like you’ve kind of cracked advertising in generative AI?

What we are seeing is as people ask longer queries, they’re specifying more of their intent. What are they really trying to do? What’s important to them? And that sort of allows new opportunities to think about ads targeting.

There’s some efforts like direct offers, in which…the advertiser can give a more specific ad for you based on what it is. And so, an example is like you’re searching for a hotel, you’re searching with a family. Maybe a hotel wants to offer free breakfast. They’re not going to give free breakfast to the person that they think is traveling for business who will just pay, or they won’t eat. But this family might pick that hotel because of it, and so Google’s system will allow [the hotel] to say, “Oh, I have a special discount just for you for breakfast,” and that really provides new value to the user and sort of allows the hotel to get additional visitors. We both have something that’s working, and there’s lots of room for innovation going forward.

There’s always been some level of slop on the internet, and I know Google has tools to sift through that. But as generative AI tools have created this ability to churn out more content, how do you make sure that with things like the AI Overviews, the accuracy is maintained? And have you seen the accuracy of those go up overall?

To your point, there’s always been slop. Sometimes people are like, “Oh, there’s now slop on the web.” In my experience, there’s been slop for 20 years. So we have a lot of experience and teams whose job is to ensure that both we’re getting rid of spam and that that rarely surfaces, and that high-quality content continues to surface. And when we do AI Overviews or AI Mode, we actually make use of those underlying search ranking systems so that it’s the highest-quality sites going into AI Overviews. Overall, the quality of the AI Overviews has continued to improve and has improved considerably since we first launched. The models are much better, for one, so that really helps. But also, we’ve just learned a lot and continue to grow on what the techniques are [and] how you work with the models to ensure that you can actually really ground the data in high-quality information.

Are Gemini and AI Mode search still different experiences, or are they converging into the same thing?

We think of them as having two different North Stars. Gemini is really focused on being this assistant, and search AI Mode is really focused on a generative AI search experience. And so for search, that means the importance of connecting to the web is vital. And so the way that we show the web is different…we tend to focus on information use cases more heavily. Versus with Gemini, we’ll focus on a lot of productivity and creativity use cases.

The use cases overlap. We have a view that you should meet users where you are, so you don’t go and say, like, “Oops, you asked the question in the wrong product. Try again.” We will try and answer across both of them the full breadth of questions that come to our products, but we will tune them differently, and really tune search to focus on optimizing for information use cases and optimizing for connecting people to the web.

Where is Google search headed in the long term, and what are some of the biggest ways we can expect it to change further?

There’s a couple of things that we see. Experiences are becoming more personal and custom for you, for each one. It’s not just that you can ask that longer question, but that we start to understand how to make information most useful for you. We see people learn differently. We have people who love videos and people who hate videos. We have people who are experts in the financial jargon and not in the medical jargon. We have people who speak different languages.

And so, with some of the things like generative UI…the job is not just for you to technically access information, but for it to be useful to you—that’s an important part of the mission. How do we present information in ways that are much more useful? That sense of building a thing that feels designed for you, and not just designed for 2 billion people, to make it easier for you to understand and grasp the information will continue.

Also, agents and how they show up in search in terms of just, how do they offload more of the work you don’t want to do? I think people have parts of searching where they enjoy and they’re delighted, and then they have parts of tasks that feel like there’s a lot of toil. And so, how can you offload those parts, and then make it easy for people to spend their time on the things they want to enjoy?

We’ll see that people will ask harder and harder questions. That’s been the evolution of search. You get better at answering the question. They’re like, “OK, I’m gonna raise the bar on you,” and so I think we’ll continue to see people go more and more to, what’s the real question they’re trying to get done, what’s the task they’re trying to get done.

item.title: This startup wants a robot to change your tires
item.dc:creator: Jordyn Grzelewski
item.description: One of the problems ATI aims to help solve is a growing shortage of automotive service technicians.
item.content:encoded:
Getting your car’s tires changed is the automotive service equivalent of getting a root canal.

That’s how Andy Chalofsky, CEO of newly launched AI and robotics company Automated Tire, Inc., or ATI, thinks of it—and why he and his fellow co-founders decided to use an emerging technology to disrupt a process that’s historically been cumbersome, time-consuming, and physically demanding.

“While the auto industry has made great strides with advanced technologies over recent decades, automotive service bays have seen little innovation to match,” Chalofsky said in a statement Tuesday announcing ATI’s emergence from stealth.

“Most notably, electric vehicles wear through tires up to 30% faster,” he added. “The proliferation of EVs creates significantly more tire service opportunities, but tire technician jobs are dirty, injury-prone, and difficult to fill.”

Get smart: Enter SmartBay, ATI’s platform that uses robotics, machine learning, and computer vision to automate services including tire changes, wheel balancing, and vehicle inspections. The startup touts SmartBay as a way to increase repair shops’ efficiency, improve the customer experience, and help solve a nagging automotive technician shortage.

Here’s how it works: Once a vehicle is in position, the platform automatically begins an inspection. It analyzes tire and wheel conditions while gathering diagnostic data. “The robotic system then executes the tire change and wheel balancing process, removing and reinstalling tires with consistent accuracy while simultaneously calculating and applying precise wheel weights to ensure optimal balance,” according to a news release.

According to ATI, SmartBay allows one technician to manage up to three service bays at a time, reducing the time for a full tire service job by half. The product fits within a standard 12-foot service bay.

So tire-d: Chalofsky represents the fourth generation of his family to work in the tire business. He started working in tire distribution and went on to establish an online tire retailer that he later sold. In 2020, he said, he started to think about the next industry challenge he wanted to focus on.

“We just saw that there was a real need in installation, and tire changing and wheel balancing,” he told us. “It’s not a very pleasurable customer experience. We would talk to the shops and the shops would oftentimes talk about how hard it was to get labor.”

ATI cited a report from the National Automotive Dealers Association identifying a shortage of 37,000 automotive service technicians. This shortage affects drivers, ATI argued, by leading to “inconsistent service quality and even more grueling wait times.”

“We’re making not only that technician more efficient—we’re making them more profitable for them and the shop. And we’re also making it an easier job with a lower threshold of skill,” Chalofsky said. “You’re now taking the workforce and you’re allowing them to fill in the gap a little bit and do a job they’d actually rather do.”

He noted that repair shops and dealers employ highly skilled mechanics who are trained to work on vehicles that are becoming ever more complex. Rather than having these skilled workers do tire changes and vehicle inspections, they can focus on more lucrative and specialized service jobs.

“By segmenting that work, we’re allowing those…technicians to really focus on the more complicated vehicles and the more complicated problems,” Chalofsky said.

Problem, meet solution: Chalofsky believes that starting with a problem, then devising a solution, differentiates ATI’s approach from other tech startups.

“The most common tech story is these smart people that are into robotics or into engineering. They’re solving problems, and then they’re taking it to an industry to try to get a product-market fit,” he said. “The thing that defines us is the opposite: We have robotics and engineering talent, of course, but are really founded with deep automotive tire expertise. And we focused on solving a problem and bringing engineering to that problem, rather than engineering and then trying to bring the industry to the problem.”
